assertions.text: Multiple @TableTest methods are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing all splitting rules.
Each @TableTest has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns.
assertions.evidence: First table has 6 rows (including interaction case 'Delivery split by address, plus a separate pickup item'); spec lists 4 obligations, one optional interaction. Second table has 6 rows where 3 obligations exist (in-stock not held for backordered AND separately for pre-ordered is redundant under two-state model).

assertions.text: Fulfillment method splitting is represented as its own @TableTest — items with different fulfillment types (store pickup vs home delivery) cannot share a shipment.
assertions.evidence: splitsShipmentsByFulfillmentTypeAndAddress includes row 'Delivery and pickup items always split' with camera (DELIVERY) and mug (PICKUP) producing separate shipments

assertions.text: Delivery address splitting is represented as its own @TableTest — items going to different addresses must be in separate shipments.
assertions.evidence: splitsShipmentsByFulfillmentTypeAndAddress includes row 'Same type, different delivery addresses' with camera (Addr-A) and watch (Addr-B) producing separate shipments

assertions.text: Availability splitting is represented as its own @TableTest — in-stock items ship immediately, backordered/pre-ordered items ship when available.
assertions.evidence: splitsShipmentsByStockAvailability has 6 rows isolating availability; row 'In-stock item not held for a backordered item' shows camera (IN_STOCK) and lens (BACKORDERED) in separate shipments with IMMEDIATE and WHEN_AVAILABLE tags

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation (minimising shipments) is represented as its own @TableTest — choosing which warehouses to ship from to minimise total shipment count.
assertions.evidence: choosesWarehouseCombinationMinimizingShipmentCount has 4 rows; row 'Correct warehouse pair must be found, not just any pair' proves minimal-cover logic with W1+W3 as the only valid two-warehouse cover

assertions.text: Companion product grouping is represented as its own @TableTest — paired items (e.g. camera body and lens) should ship together from the same location when possible.
assertions.evidence: keepsCompanionProductsTogetherWhenPossible has 3 rows; row 'Companions win a tie between equally minimal warehouses' shows companions breaking a tie, row 'Companions split when no warehouse stocks both' shows preference yielding

assertions.text: Each @TableTest method includes all output columns for its concern in the same table — e.g. warehouse allocation includes both the assignment and shipment count, not split across methods.
assertions.evidence: choosesWarehouseCombinationMinimizingShipmentCount includes W1/W2/W3 Stock columns and Shipments? in one table; keepsCompanionProductsTogetherWhenPossible includes Companions and Shipments? together
